newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Burnt EBRD criticises Slovak privatisation. [CORRECTED 16:25 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Burnt EBRD criticises Slovak privatisation. [CORRECTED 16:25 GMT]

text.p: The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) has criticised Slovakia's privatisation programme as murky, and admitted that the bank itself got burnt in Bratislava.
In the past two years, Slovakia has scrapped mass voucher privatisation and sold off stakes in a number of leading companies without public tenders.
Few details of the sales are ever revealed and the names of the buyers, sometimes linked to the companies' management, rarely mean anything -- even to Slovak market watchers.
The EBRD's representative in Slovakia, Jaromir Cekota, criticised the lack information made available.
"We see that in the privatisation process important information is disclosed neither to the public nor to business partners," Cekota told a seminar on Monday.
Cekota cited the EBRD's investment in Slovak oil refiner Slovnaft a.s..
"We burnt our fingers when we bought into Slovnaft," he said at the seminar, held to discuss an Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) report on Slovakia.
Cekota was reacting to comments from a senior official of the state privatisation body, the National Property Fund (NPF).
Jan Porvaznik, an NPF executive director, told the meeting that some discrepancies in the privatisation process had been caused by the change in method from the voucher scheme.
The EBRD took a 10.5 percent stake in Slovnaft in 1995 when it bought half the refiner's $113 million issue of global depositary receipts which flopped on international markets.
The London-based development bank, set up to encourage free market reforms in post-communist Europe, effectively paid the 1,000 crowns ($32.09) (corrects currency conversion) per share face value.
But shortly afterwards, the NPF sold another 39 percent of Slovnaft to a management-led consortium called Slovintegra at an implied prices of just 156 crowns per share.

Last month the EBRD said it was close to reaching a deal with the Slovak government on selling its stake back to the NPF. Since then nothing has happened and neither Cekota nor Porvaznik would comment on how the negotiations stood.
Privatisation is one of the hottest political issues in Slovakia with the opposition alleging cronyism which the government denies.
The latest row has blown up over the sale of a 45.9 stake in monopoly oil and gas storage company Nafta Gbely a.s. NAFT.BV to little-known firm Druha Obchodna a.s..
The price was for the stake, which has a market price about 3.2 billion crowns, was 500 million crowns. The NPF has offered no explanation.
